prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and for taking them to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: After reading all eight round-1 statements my preferred configuration is unchanged: B012 alone, Katori and Ye. What changed is how I state the credit, not the choice. The scientific core is the one thing every member describes the same way, and I can vouch for it from my own field: the magic-wavelength condition cancels the lattice light shift, Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil broadening, and thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel on an ultranarrow optical transition. Parallel interrogation is why stability and accuracy improve together, and it is what separates this from the comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012). The 1e-18 level has been reached and reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in several laboratories, which is a demonstrated result and not a prospect. I do not count the eight-way agreement as evidence. Four members moved to B012 after reading the opening ballots, and I opened with it first, so I looked for a reason to doubt it. The substantive objections (incrementalism, other groups, timing) are real but none removes the invention, and a two-name credit keeps the prize clear of the three-person squeeze that Higgs and IceCube face.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is boundary and priority, not maturity. I overstated in round 1 that the credit is cleanly bounded. Five colleagues (Danielsson, Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Pearce) correctly say that the 2005 and 2012 prizes mark what is already honoured and do not show who else built lattice clocks. Other lattice-clock groups at SYRTE, PTB, and elsewhere in Boulder, plus Takamoto, are not credited, and the early history of the magic-wavelength proposal and of the first realisations rests on our recollection, not on the supplied record. A second objection is that a precision capability may be weighed below a discovery about nature or a new class of matter, which I answer by weighting, not by dismissal. A third is timing: the redefinition of the second has not happened. I treat that as a confirmation of impact and not a precondition, since the physics has already motivated it. My field bias also remains: as a laser spectroscopist I may overrate how decisive systematic-shift control is.

responses.point: Johansson agrees with the two-name structure but says the credit is not cleanly bounded and proposes writing the citation around the invention and its realisation, not a single record-accuracy number, so the prize does not appear to settle priority among lattice-clock laboratories.
responses.response: I accept the correction and have changed the citation accordingly. The citation I now propose names the invention and the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms as the credited object, and mentions the 1e-18 level only as a consequence of Ye's work, not as the thing awarded. That anchors the prize to the mechanism, which is where Katori's contribution sits, and avoids appearing to arbitrate between laboratories at the accuracy frontier. Your argument that Katori's idea without Ye's systematic control would not have reached 1e-18 is also my reason for crediting both together and not splitting the prize into a proposal and a record. I still do not think a citation can honestly claim more than that, and I would not let it claim less.

responses.point: Lindroth says the credit is clean for the invention but not for the whole subject, because ion-clock groups and NIST, PTB and SYRTE built much of the field's maturity, and she asks whether lattice and ion clocks need joint recognition.
responses.response: Your distinction between a clean invention and a not-clean subject is the right one, and it replaces my phrase about a cleanly bounded credit. I would still not bundle ion clocks. Wineland's 2012 recognition covers control of single quantum systems, and adding an ion-clock laureate would give an unclear boundary, probably a fourth name, and a metrology prize in place of an invention prize. On your remark about B010, I concede the point: the Cirac-Zoller idea is decisive but the experimental credit is spread over several ion-trap groups, and the 2012 overlap is real. I have therefore moved B010 behind B003 in my alternatives and I would not advance it without a sharper citation.

responses.point: Olsson regards the novelty margin over combs and ion clocks as the main reservation and also asks how much weight to give prospective impacts such as the redefinition of the second against demonstrated results.
responses.response: On weighting I side with demonstrated results and would judge the prize on those: orders-of-magnitude gains in systematic control, independent confirmation across Sr, Yb and Hg, and clock comparisons at the 1e-18 level. The redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and searches for varying constants are consequences that make the result more interesting, but I would not let them carry the case, and I would not postpone a prize until an administrative decision by metrology bodies is made. On novelty margin I think the comb and the single ion are the wrong comparison: neither contains a many-atom ensemble interrogated without a light shift. Where I respect your position is that this is a judgment the committee makes, and I would want it written into the citation instead of assumed.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B012 from IceCube and argues that the citation should name the lattice clock specifically so it does not overreach into ion or microwave standards, and that the redefinition of the second should not be a condition.
responses.response: We agree on both points and the revised citation follows your first one: it says optical lattice clocks and magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and does not speak of optical clocks in general. On your reservation about B010, you and Lindroth have persuaded me that the experimental credit there is too diffuse, and I now list B003 first among my alternatives. I would add one caution for B029, which you raise as a later candidate: the AMANDA and Baikal precursors and the fair allocation among Halzen, Karle and Spiering would need to be settled from the record before it can compete, and I cannot do that from my own field.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B039 to B012 and keeps B039 as the principal alternative, saying the Higgs observation is overdue and the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist, but that he cannot defend a three-name selection from the record.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs observation is first-rate and mature, and I do not rank it lower for lack of merit. Our difference is how much the credit problem should weigh. You say you cannot defend any three-name set from the record, and neither can I: the choice between Della Negra and Virdee, and between Jenni and Gianotti, rests on leadership roles and not on identifiable scientific authorship. That is a statutory problem for the prize, not a flaw in the discovery, and it is why B039 is not my preferred configuration this year. I would not call it weaker science. If the committee found a principled rule for credit I would be willing to hear the argument, but I do not see one in the supplied record.

responses.point: Mehlig says the boundary needs care, that Boulder, Paris, PTB and other groups made important lattice-clock contributions, and that the citation should be worded around the invention and realisation and the record performance, not around all precision optical clocks.
responses.response: That is the wording I now propose, and I thank you for it. On your second choice I note that B057 is conceptually deep, but I share your doubt that the credit holds: the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the three-dimensional work with Fu. I do not rule it out for a later year. One disagreement with your framing: you say the redefinition of the second has no bearing on the science. I agree, and would go a little further and say it should not enter the committee's assessment at all, except as context.

uncertainties: Priority and relative roles of Katori and Ye in the magic-wavelength proposal and early realisations are not settled by the supplied record. We are working from general knowledge. In answer to the chair, I cannot verify this and the committee should check primary publications before a final ballot.
Whether other lattice-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, Boulder colleagues, Takamoto) have a claim of the same standing as the two credited names that a three-person cap would force us to exclude.
Whether the committee judges the step beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes sufficient. I think it is, but this is a judgment about novelty and not a measured fact.

If B012 is not chosen, whether B003 (credit contested over Chu) or B010 (credit diffuse, 2012 overlap) is the stronger atomic-physics fallback. I now rate both as weaker than B012 and none as clearly stronger than the other.
statement.conflict_note: No documented collaboration with Katori or Ye and no tie to B012. In response to the chair's question, my remote connection stands as disclosed in round 1: I spent time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Ye's work belongs to the same precision-spectroscopy lineage. It is a lineage connection, not a collaboration, and I do not think it requires recusal, but I leave that ruling to the chair and would accept any decision. Hall's 2005 prize is the neighbouring recognition I cite as a boundary, so I have been careful to argue it on the physics. My Lund colleagues, WACQT and Deep Light Vision ties do not touch B012, B003 or B010.
